_doc: T-3645: every building card's opening line, as the floating card and Inspect's Overview show it (tools/reading_leads.mjs), retold for younger readers. Keyed by the line's own words, since many buildings share a composed line. Only the younger ages are written; no fact enters that the line does not hold, and the build's own talk (record ids, kit names, pixel readings) is left out.

8-10: A Kinzie store on South Water Street. A history book says it was there by 1833. In 1834 it moved other men's goods. It took them off the ships and sent them on inland. That was what South Water Street was for.
11-13: A Kinzie store on South Water Street. Andreas names it as one of three stores there by 1833. In 1834 it was a forwarding store. That means it took other men's goods off the ships and sent them inland. That was what South Water Street was for.
14-15: A Kinzie store on South Water Street. Andreas names it as one of three there by 1833. In 1834 it traded as a forwarding and commission house. That was the business of taking other men's goods off the schooners and getting them inland, which is what South Water Street was for.

8-10: A food store run by Jones on South Water Street. It put an ad in the very first copy of the town paper, in November 1833. It still had ads in 1834. By then it also moved other men's goods for them.
11-13: A grocery store run by Jones on South Water Street. It put an ad in the first issue of the Chicago Democrat, in November 1833. It was still placing ads in 1834. By then, Andreas says, it also shipped other men's goods for them.
14-15: A grocery and provision store run by Jones on South Water Street. It advertised in the first issue of the Chicago Democrat in November 1833. It was still among the town's advertisers in 1834. By then, Andreas says, it was also doing forwarding and commission work.

8-10: The jail keeper's own house. A man named Gale wrote about it. It stood partly inside the jail's fence, and it faced Randolph Street. Its look is a best guess. It comes from an old picture of 1836. The old log jail is still the jail. Its roof was not picked from pictures that do not agree.
11-13: The jail keeper's house, which Gale describes. It stood partly inside the jail's fence and faced Randolph Street. It is a best guess, based on a picture from 1836. The new house does not change what the old log jail is. Its roof was not chosen from pictures that do not agree.
14-15: A separate house for the jail keeper, described by Gale. It stood partly inside the jail fence and faced Randolph Street. It is included as a reconstruction, and the 1836 date on the picture is left as it is. The new house does not relabel the old log jail, and its roof is not picked from pictures that disagree.

8-10: A stable behind the Sauganash Hotel. Its size comes from how many beds the hotel had. It stands on its own patch of ground.

A stable behind the Wolf Point Tavern. In 1831 the county set a price for keeping a horse overnight at the two inns in Chicago. This was one of them. No one wrote down how big the stable was, what it was made of, or where it stood. So this stable is a guess from a price list.
11-13: A stable behind the Wolf Point Tavern. In 1831 Cook County set a price for keeping a horse overnight at the two Chicago inns. This was one of them, so it must have had a stable. Nothing is known about the stable's size, what it was made of or where it stood. It is a guess from a price list.
14-15: A stable behind the Wolf Point Tavern. A Cook County price list of 13 April 1831 set the cost of keeping a horse overnight at the two Chicago inns, and this was one of them. Nothing is recorded about the stable's size, materials or position. The building is a reading of a price list.

8-10: W. H. Stow built this in 1834 at the corner of Randolph and Canal. The front was 40 feet wide. A wing 60 feet long made an L shape. There was a big stable, and a yard where wagons drove in. It was open and busy in July 1835.
Tents on the bank of South Water Street, where new settlers got off the boats. The paper said there were "some," so only a few are here.
Tents of new settlers on the shore by the fort. They were moved here, off the docks on South Water Street.

George W. Dole's warehouse and meat yard of 1832, near Lake and Dearborn. He and a partner shipped goods. Their other warehouse was across the river. Dole packed the first beef and pork sent out of Chicago. By 1834 the partners had a new meat house on the river. So this yard had likely stopped by July 1835.
11-13: George W. Dole's warehouse and slaughter yard of 1832, near Lake and Dearborn. It was the south side of the shipping business of Newberry and Dole. Their other warehouse and dock were on the north bank. Dole packed the first beef and pork shipped out of Chicago. By 1834 the partners had built a meat house on the South Branch. So the killing had likely left this yard by July 1835.
14-15: George W. Dole's warehouse and slaughter yard of 1832, near the Lake and Dearborn crossing. It was the south-side half of the Newberry and Dole shipping business, whose other warehouse and wharf were on the north bank. Dole packed the first beef and pork shipped out of Chicago. By 1834 the partners had built a slaughterhouse on the South Branch, so the killing had probably left this yard by the scene date.

8-10: It was a wood warehouse. Goods were stored here and shipped on for other men. The Dole family worked here.
11-13: It was a light wood warehouse that shipped goods for other men. The Dole household worked here.

8-10: It was a log building where meat was cut and packed. It was built in 1827. The Clybourne family worked here.
It was a wood building, one floor high. A paper was printed here. The Davis family of the American worked here.
It was a wood shop, one floor high. Saddles and harness for horses were made here. Goss and Cobb worked here.
It was a brick hotel, one floor high. It was still being built.
It was a small brick building where gunpowder was kept. It was one floor high.
It was a log house, one floor high. The man who dealt with the Native people for the government worked here. It had stood like this since 1820. The Caldwell family worked here.
It was a wood store, two floors high. It was here by 1833. The Calhoun family worked here.
It was a wood store, two floors high. The Harmon brothers worked here.
It was a brick house two floors high. The man in charge of the fort lived here with his family.
11-13: It was a two-story brick house for the fort's commanding officer. His family lived here.

8-10: It was a log house, two floors high, and a trading store. Jean Baptiste Beaubien and his family lived and worked here.
It was a log house two floors high, where soldiers lived. A soldier named Edward Cavanagh lived here. His wife, Honora Duffy, and their kids lived here too.
11-13: It was a two-story log barracks for soldiers. A married soldier of the first company lived here: Edward Cavanagh, with Honora Duffy and their children.

8-10: It was a log house two floors high. The fort's doctor and his family lived here.

Mark Beaubien's own log cabin, called the Eagle Exchange, from 1829. It stood at Lake and Market. In 1831 he built a bigger hotel onto it. After that he rented the cabin out. In 1832 Philo Carpenter opened the town's first drug store here. He soon moved out. Next John S. Wright rented it. In 1833 Eliza Chappel ran a school here. In 1834 her school moved to a church. By July 1835 all three were gone. No one wrote down what the room was used for then, or who was in it.
11-13: Mark Beaubien's own log cabin, the Eagle Exchange of 1829, at Lake and Market. In 1831 he built the wood Sauganash Hotel onto it, and from then on he rented the cabin out. Philo Carpenter opened Chicago's first drug store in it in 1832 and soon moved out. Next Beaubien rented it to John S. Wright. From September 1833 it held Eliza Chappel's school, which moved into a church in 1834. By July 1835 all three were gone, and no source says what the room was used for, or who was in it.
14-15: Mark Beaubien's own log cabin, the Eagle Exchange of 1829, still standing at the Lake and Market corner after the frame Sauganash was built onto it in 1831. From then on it was rented out. Philo Carpenter opened Chicago's first drug store in it in late summer 1832 and soon moved out. Beaubien then rented it to John S. Wright. From September 1833 it held Eliza Chappel's school, which moved into the First Presbyterian Church in 1834. By 1 July 1835 all three uses are over, and no source says what the room was doing or names anyone in it.

8-10: This is one Beaubien house, with a barn and a trading post. A man named Wentworth wrote a note under an old picture from 1831. It puts a Beaubien house near this corner. That is our best guess. We do not know how old the house is or how it looked. The Factor's House stands on its own, about 140 meters south. Beaubien asked for the land on 28 May 1835. It was written down on 26 June. Later work checked the house against pictures. It has two floors, two roofs, a low part in front, and one small window up high. Its size and what it was made of are still not known.
11-13: This is one Beaubien house, with a barn and a trading post. Wentworth's note under the 1831 picture puts a Beaubien house near this corner. That is a best guess from the same man who told of the sale. When it was built and how it looked are not known. The Factor's House is a separate building, about 140 meters south, and its two floors are not copied here. Beaubien's claim to the land was dated 28 May 1835 and written down on 26 June. Later work checked the house against pictures. It now has two floors, two roofs, a low part in front and a small window high in one end. Its size, what it was made of and where it faced are still not known.
14-15: Modelled as one Beaubien house with a barn and trading post. Wentworth's note under the 1831 picture places a Beaubien house near this corner. That is an inferred match from the same witness who told of the sale. The building's history, its year and its look remain unknown. The Factor's House is modelled on its own, about 140 meters south, and its two-story description is not copied here. Beaubien's claim to the land was dated 28 May 1835 and recorded on 26 June. Later work compared the house with pictures. It now has a two-level main part with two roofs, one low front part and one small attic window in the right end. Exact sizes, materials, hidden openings and which way it faced are still not known.

8-10: This building was sold twice in this time. Jouett sold it to Dean when the fort was built again. In 1822 the government sold it to a fur company, and Beaubien moved in. None of the three people who wrote about it say the building changed. So nothing here is tied to those sales. The name comes from the old map.
11-13: One stage, but the building changed hands twice in it. Jouett sold it to Dean when the fort was rebuilt. Then in 1822 the United States sold it to the American Fur Company, and Beaubien moved in. None of the three people who wrote about it say the building changed. So nothing here is dated to those sales. The name is the one on the old map.
14-15: One stage, and the building changed hands twice inside it. Jouett sold to Dean when the fort was built the second time. Then in 1822 the United States sold it to the American Fur Company, and Beaubien moved in. None of the three witnesses describe any change to the building, so nothing here is dated to those sales. The name is the one the old map gives it.

8-10: On 1 July 1835 a hotel is being built here. A notice from 10 June says so. How far along it is is a guess. The brick walls are uneven and have no roof yet. There are open gaps and two wood stands inside. It sits on a plan 24 by 15 meters, and it is up to 4 meters tall. The roof, top tower, windows and sign from a later picture are not shown yet.
11-13: On 1 July 1835 a hotel is being built here, as a notice of 10 June shows. How far along it is is a best guess. The brick walls are uneven, with no roof, open gaps and two wood stands inside. It sits on the 24 by 15 meter plan, at most 4 meters tall. The finished roof, tower, glass windows, sign and rooms from the later picture are not shown before their time.
14-15: On 1 July 1835 a hotel is being built here, as the 10 June notice shows. Its stage is a reconstruction: uneven brick walls with no roof, open work gaps and two timber stands inside, on the 24 by 15 meter plan, at most 4 meters high. The finished hotel's roof, tower, glass, sign and rooms are not taken back in time from the later picture.

8-10: One stage only. Neither person who wrote about this barn says it changed. To split it up would be to make up a story.
One stage only. Neither person who wrote about it says this building changed.
One stage only. The old map shows buildings like this on this bank. But no one named this one. So it has no history to split up. Making one up would be making things up twice.
11-13: One stage only. This is a building of a kind the map puts on this bank, not one that anyone named. So it has no history to split into stages. Making one up would mean making things up twice.

8-10: One stage only. The old maps show buildings like this on this bank. But no one named this one. So it has no history to split up. Making one up would be making things up twice.
11-13: One stage only. This is a building of a kind the maps put on this bank, not one that anyone named. So it has no history to split into stages. Making one up would mean making things up twice.

8-10: One stage only. The plant's own record says one of its buildings is missing. This is our guess at it. No one named it, so it has no history to split up. Making one up would be making things up twice.
11-13: One stage only. The plant's own record says one of its work buildings is missing, and this is a rebuilt guess at it. No one named it, so it has no history to split into stages. Making one up would mean making things up twice.

8-10: One look only, because the record tells of just one. It was a log bridge where Water Street crossed the swamp. It stood until after 1840. No one wrote that it was fixed, made wider or replaced. That is because the record is thin. It does not mean the bridge stayed the same for seven years over wet ground.
11-13: One look only, because the record describes one: a log bridge where Water Street crossed the slough, until after 1840. Nothing says it was rebuilt, widened or replaced in that time. That is a gap in what we know. It is not a claim that it stood untouched for seven years over wet ground.
14-15: One state, because the source describes one: a log bridge, needed where Water Street crossed the slough, until after 1840. Nothing records it being rebuilt, widened or replaced in that time. That is a limit of the evidence, not a claim that it stood untouched for seven years over wet ground.

8-10: One look only, because there is just one paper about it. An ad from 26 November 1833 is all we know of this store. Nothing tells of it before or after.
11-13: One look only, because there is just one record. The ad of 26 November 1833 is all we know of this business. Nothing describes it before or after.

8-10: One look only. Nothing at all tells of this crossing. So nothing tells of it being built again. It is shown as one best guess on 1 July 1835. That does not mean it never changed.
One look only, because there is nothing to split up. Nothing tells when it was built, how it looked or how it changed.
A freight shed on a street on the south side. It was added to fill a gap. No other building was moved for it.
11-13: One of the freight sheds owed to a street on the south side. It was added without moving any other building.

8-10: The seventh freight shed on the north side of the river. It was added to fill a gap. No other building was moved for it.
11-13: The seventh freight shed on the north side of the river. It was added without moving any other building.
14-15: The seventh freight shed in the North Division. It was added without moving any building that was already there.

8-10: A wood shed on a street on the south side. It was added to fill a gap. No other building was moved for it.
11-13: The lumber shed owed to a street on the south side. It was added without moving any other building.

8-10: The second of two freight sheds planned for the west side of the river. It was added to fill a gap. No other building was moved for it. It is on block 50, one step back from the river. It faces the river, between the block and the bank.
11-13: The second of the two freight sheds planned for the west side of the river. It was added without moving any other building. It sits on block 50, one step inland, on the river side of the block, between it and the bank.
14-15: The second of the two freight sheds the plan gives the West Division. It was added without moving any other building. It stands on block 50, one step inland, on the river face of the block between it and the bank.

8-10: The second freight shed on the west side of the river. It was added to fill a gap. No other building was moved for it.
11-13: The second freight shed on the west side of the river. It was added without moving any other building.
14-15: The second freight shed in the West Division. It was added without moving any building that was already there.

8-10: A store building. It is a best guess. It was added to fill a gap. No other building was moved for it.
11-13: A rebuilt guess at a store building. It was added without moving any other building.
14-15: A reconstructed store building. It was added without moving any building that was already there.

8-10: A store in a row of shops in the middle of town. It is a guess. If a better known building turns up, it will take this one's place.
11-13: A store that fills the row of shops in the middle of town. A better known building will take its place, so the town does not grow.
14-15: A store raised to fill the rows of shops in the middle of town. A better known building takes its place rather than adding to the town.

8-10: A small change to how this looks. The front yard stays the same. The old back wing is gone. Now there is an open bay for wagons, a link, and a long wing where people stayed. Another plan, with a closed end, is kept on its own. The dates and the place are still not sure.
11-13: A small change to how this looks. The front yard stays as it was. The old back wing is replaced by an open wagon bay, a link and a long wing where boarders stayed. Another plan, with a closed end, is kept on its own and not used here. The dates, the place and the whole picture are still not sure.
14-15: A small change to how this looks. The front yard stays as it was, and the old rear wing is replaced by an open wagon bay, a link and a turned wing for boarders. The closed-end version is kept as a separate idea and is not used here. The dates, the place and the whole picture are still not sure.

8-10: This was added for a family that likely lived here. If a better known building turns up, it will take this one's place.
11-13: This was added for a family that likely lived here. A better known building will take its place, not stand beside it.

8-10: A guess at a building with no name, on the north side in July 1835. If a better known building turns up, it will take this one's place. That way the town stays at 665 roofs.
11-13: A rebuilt guess at an unnamed building on the north side in July 1835. A better known building can take its place, so the town stays at 665 roofs.
14-15: A reconstructed building with no name, filling the North Division in July 1835. A better-known building can take its place, so the town's total stays at 665 roofs.

8-10: A guess at a building with no name, on the west side in July 1835. If a better known building turns up, it will take this one's place. That way the town stays at 665 roofs.
11-13: A rebuilt guess at an unnamed building on the west side in July 1835. A better known building can take its place, so the town stays at 665 roofs.
14-15: A reconstructed building with no name, filling the West Division in July 1835. A better-known building can take its place, so the town's total stays at 665 roofs.

8-10: A guess at a building with no name, on this block in July 1835. If a better known building turns up, it will take this one's place. That way the town stays at 665 roofs.
11-13: A rebuilt guess at an unnamed building on this block in July 1835. A better known building can take its place, so the town stays at 665 roofs.
14-15: A reconstructed building with no name, filling this block in July 1835. A better-known building can take its place, so the town's total stays at 665 roofs.

8-10: A guess at a building with no name, in July 1835. Later, a better known building may take its place.
11-13: A rebuilt guess at an unnamed building in July 1835. Later, a better known building may take its place.
14-15: A reconstructed building with no name, in July 1835. Later a named, better-known building may take its place.

8-10: The government's blacksmith shop. It stood near the agency house, at the end of State Street. It was here from about 1823. That year David McKee came to be the blacksmith. A treaty of 1821 said there must be one. Later McKee carried the mail, and then he moved away. Those were changes in his work, not in the shop.
11-13: The government's blacksmith shop at the Chicago agency. It stood near the agency house at the foot of State Street from about 1823. That year David McKee came to fill the job that the 1821 treaty called for. Later McKee carried the mail and moved to the Des Plaines River. Those were changes in his work, not changes to the shop.
14-15: The government blacksmith's shop of the Chicago agency. It stood near the agency house at the foot of State Street from about 1823, when David McKee arrived to fill the job the 1821 treaty required. McKee's later work as a mail carrier and his move to the Des Plaines are changes of work. They do not start new stages for the shop.

8-10: The government's agency house on the north bank, as a book called Wau-Bun tells of it in 1831. It was made of logs cut square. It had a middle part, two side wings and two parts out back. After 1823, boards were put on part of the walls. It stood at the end of State Street and faced the river. By 1831 a new street ran behind it. Wolcott, who ran it, died in 1830. After that, other people used it. But the house itself did not change.
11-13: The government's Indian Agency house on the north bank, as Wau-Bun tells of it in 1831. It was built of logs cut square, with a middle part, two side wings and two back parts. Sometime after 1823, boards were put partway up its walls. It stood at the foot of State Street, facing the river, and by 1831 a new street ran across its back. After Wolcott died in 1830, other people used it. That was a change of use, not of the house.
14-15: The United States Indian Agency house on the north bank, as Wau-Bun describes it in 1831. It was hewn square log, with a center, two wings and two rear parts. Sometime after 1823 boards were put partway up its walls. It stood at the foot of State Street with its front to the river, and by 1831 a laid-out street ran across its back. The changes of who lived there after Wolcott's death in 1830 are changes of use. They do not start new stages.

8-10: The log jail, built in the fall of 1833. On 1 July 1835 it is still the only county building we know of. The keeper's house, the fence and the roof are our best guess. They come from what Gale said and from an old picture of 1836. The roof is 3.35 meters high at the edge, and it slopes at 28 degrees. There is one window up in the end wall, as in the picture. The size is a guess. The later courthouse and any new cell are not shown.
11-13: The log jail of fall 1833 is still the only county building we know of on 1 July 1835. The keeper's house, the fence and the main roof are a best guess. They come from Gale's memory of 1835 and a picture marked 1836. The roof edge is 3.35 meters high and slopes at 28 degrees, in place of the old low guess. One window sits up in the end wall, as the picture shows. The size is a best guess. The footprint, the walls and the dates stay as they were. No later courthouse, extra cell or new family is added.
14-15: The log jail of fall 1833 is still the only known county building on 1 July 1835. The keeper's house, the fence and the main roof are reconstructed from Gale's memory of 1835 and the detailed picture marked 1836. The roof edge at 3.35 meters and a 28-degree pitch replace the earlier low stand-in, and one upright window in the end wall follows the picture. Exact sizes are reconstructed. The footprint, walls, dates and setback stay as they were, with no later courthouse, extra cell or new household brought back in time.

8-10: The barn that the ad lists along with the house.
The building as far as we know it in July 1835. Where old records give its size, plan or what it was made of, we use that. Where they do not, the notes say so.

A building at the corner of Lake and LaSalle. A history book calls it "the old bank building." In 1834 Gurdon S. Hubbard packed about five thousand hogs here. That was the start of the meat trade that later made the city big. We do not know what it was used for in July 1835. And the name here is one that Chicago only used later.
11-13: The building at Lake and LaSalle that Andreas calls "the old bank building." Gurdon S. Hubbard packed about five thousand hogs in it in 1834. That was the start of the meat trade the city was later built on. No one says what it was used for in July 1835. And its name here is one that Chicago did not use until later.
14-15: The building at the corner of Lake and LaSalle that Andreas calls "the old bank building." Gurdon S. Hubbard packed about five thousand hogs in it in the 1834 season, the start of the trade the city was later built on. What it was doing in July 1835 is not recorded, and the name it carries here is one Chicago did not use until later.

8-10: The building at South Water and Clark. Here John Calhoun set up the press that printed the Chicago Democrat. It was Chicago's first newspaper. It came out first on 26 November 1833. The building was not finished when he moved in. On 1 July 1835 the paper is almost two years old. Now there is a second paper, the Chicago American. It is just four weeks old. It is three blocks east, near the bridge.
11-13: The building at South Water and Clark where John Calhoun set up the hand press that printed the Chicago Democrat, Chicago's first newspaper, from 26 November 1833. Andreas says the building was not finished when Calhoun moved in. On 1 July 1835 the paper is twenty months old. It is one of two papers on the street. The Chicago American is four weeks old, three blocks east near the bridge.
14-15: The building at the corner of South Water and Clark where John Calhoun set up the hand press that printed the Chicago Democrat, Chicago's first newspaper, from 26 November 1833. Andreas records it as unfinished when Calhoun moved in, and the first issue gives the address. On 1 July 1835 the paper is twenty months old and one of two on the street. The Chicago American, four weeks old, is three blocks east near the drawbridge.

8-10: The cabin where Jean Baptiste Beaubien lived before 1817. Then he bought the Dean house, where the river meets the lake, and moved in. He kept the old cabin as a barn. In July 1835 it is one of the farm buildings on the fort's land. Five weeks before, he asked to own all of that land. It was about 76 acres.
11-13: The cabin Jean Baptiste Beaubien lived in before 1817. After he bought the Dean house at the mouth of the river and moved into it, he kept the cabin as a barn. In July 1835 it is one of the outbuildings of his home on the Fort Dearborn land. Five weeks earlier he claimed the whole 75.69 acres of that land.
14-15: The cabin Jean Baptiste Beaubien lived in before 1817. It was left standing and used as a barn after he bought the Dean house at the mouth of the river and moved in. In July 1835 it is one of the outbuildings of his home on the Fort Dearborn reservation, and his claim to the whole 75.69-acre reservation is five weeks old.

8-10: The cabins as the family built them and lived in them in the 1820s and 1830s. Archibald Clybourne also had a bigger house from 1829, on what is now Elston Avenue. That house is not shown here. It stood farther out, past the edge of town. No one wrote that these cabins changed.
11-13: The cabins as the family built them and lived in them through the 1820s and into the 1830s. Archibald Clybourne's bigger house of 1829, on what is now Elston Avenue, was a different building. It is not shown here. It stood farther out, past the town's edge. Nothing says these cabins changed.

8-10: The clothing store John Holbrook opened in June 1835. It was one door from Dearborn Street. It was in the empty spot that the paper's ads leave. That spot was between the paper's office on the corner and Frederick Thomas's shop.
11-13: John Holbrook opened this clothing store in the second week of June 1835. It is one door from Dearborn. The ads in the American leave this door empty. It is between the paper's office at the corner and Frederick Thomas's shop.
14-15: The clothing store John Holbrook opened one door from Dearborn in the second week of June 1835. It takes the door that the American's own ads leave empty, between the paper's office at the corner and Frederick Thomas's shop.

8-10: The drug store of Pruyne and Kimball on South Water Street. It was the town's second or third, after Philo Carpenter's. A history book gives only their names and the street. So the store is on the right street, but we do not know which lot.
11-13: The drug store of Pruyne and Kimball on South Water Street, the town's second or third, after Philo Carpenter's. Andreas gives only the partners and the street. So this is a business on the right street, not a building on a known lot.
14-15: The drug store of Pruyne and Kimball on South Water Street, the town's second or third after Philo Carpenter's. Andreas records the partners and the street and nothing else. So this record is a business placed on the right street, not a building placed on a lot.

8-10: The stray pen, built in March 1832 at one corner of the town square. It was Chicago's first public building. It held animals that got loose. There was no jail, so it held prisoners too. That stopped when the log jail was built in the fall of 1833. The pen is still here in July 1835. It has no roof now. On that day the square has only two things on it, this pen and the jail. The courthouse and the fire house came later in 1835. So the east half of the square is open grass.
11-13: The stray pen, built in March 1832 at the south-west corner of the town square. It was Chicago's first public building. It held loose farm animals, and, with nowhere else to put them, prisoners. That ended when the log jail went up in the fall of 1833. The pen is still standing on 1 July 1835. It has no roof now. Its name in the files has the wrong year, but it is kept because changing it would mean rebuilding the model. On that day the square holds only two things: this pen and the log jail. The courthouse and the fire house came later in 1835, so the east half of the square is open prairie.
14-15: The stray pen, built in March 1832 on the south-west corner of the public square. It was Chicago's first public building, put up to hold stray animals and, with nowhere else, prisoners. That ended when the log jail went up at the north-west corner in the fall of 1833. The pen is not recorded as going anywhere, and it stands on 1 July 1835. Its roof was taken off in 2026, so it stands as an open pen. Its file name still has the wrong year, but renaming it would mean a rebuild, which is not worth it for a name. On that day the square held only two things: this pen and the log jail. The courthouse and the fire house belong to later in 1835, so the east half of the square is open prairie.

8-10: The first building on the corner of South Water and Dearborn. It was a log house with two rooms. Madore Beaubien built it in 1831, when he started to sell goods. Four years later it is still a log house on the town's main shopping corner. In July 1835 South Water Street is not all new wood stores. Some old log buildings are still there too.
11-13: The first building on the south-west corner of South Water and Dearborn: a two-room log house that Madore Beaubien built in 1831, when he first became a merchant. Four years later it is still a log building on the town's main shopping corner. That is part of what 1835 shows. South Water Street in July 1835 is not a row of new wood stores. It is a mixed street, with log buildings from 1831 still on it.
14-15: The first building on Lot 1 at the south-west corner of South Water and Dearborn: a two-room log house Madore Beaubien built in 1831, when he was newly licensed as a merchant. Four years later it is a log building on the town's main shopping corner. That is part of what the 1835 scene is for. South Water Street in July 1835 is not a matching row of new frame stores, but a mixed street with 1831 log buildings still standing.

8-10: The first building on Lake Street made to be a store. It was two floors high and made of wood. Thomas Church built it. It shows that Lake Street was starting to win shoppers from South Water Street. That change took until 1836 or 1837. So in July 1835 it is just a first sign.
11-13: The first store built as a store on Lake Street, a two-story wood building put up by Thomas Church. It marks Lake Street starting to compete with South Water for the town's trade. The shift did not finish until 1836 or 1837, so in July 1835 it is an early sign.

8-10: A wood church, built in August 1833. It was ready to use in October. It was 25 by 35 feet and cost about $400. The wood came by boat from St. Joseph. Anson Taylor hauled it to the spot. Augustine D. Taylor drew it and built it. At first it had bare walls with no paint. It had rough benches and no tower. We do not know when it got bigger or got its small bell tower. So this shows it as it was at first. That is a best guess.
11-13: A wood church, raised in August 1833 and ready to use in October. It was 25 by 35 feet and cost about $400. The wood came by boat from St. Joseph, and Anson Taylor hauled it to the spot. Augustine D. Taylor designed and built it. At first it had bare, unpainted walls, rough benches and no tower. When it was made bigger and got its small bell tower is not known, so neither is shown. This first, plain look is a best guess.
14-15: The wood church raised in August 1833 and ready for use in October: 25 by 35 feet, about $400. The lumber came by boat from St. Joseph and Anson Taylor hauled it to the site. Augustine D. Taylor designed and built it. As built in 1833 it had bare, unpainted walls, rough benches and no steeple or tower. When it was enlarged and got its low open bell tower is not known, and neither is shown here. The plain early form is a best guess.

8-10: A house on the north bank, just east of Clark Street. Two colonels, Hamilton and Owen, are said to have built it for a school in 1833. John Watkins ran his school in it. He had started the school in 1832, in Hamilton's small horse stable. Later it became a free school for all. That was a change in use, not in the building.
11-13: The house Colonels Hamilton and Owen are said to have built for a school in 1833, on the north bank just east of Clark Street. John Watkins ran the school here. He had started it in 1832 in Hamilton's twelve-foot horse stable. Later it changed from a paid school to a public one. That was a change of use, not of the building.
14-15: The house Colonels Hamilton and Owen are said to have built for a school in 1833, on the north bank just east of Clark Street. John Watkins taught here in the school he had begun in 1832 in Hamilton's twelve-foot horse stable. Its change from a paid school to a public school is a change of use. It does not start a new stage.

8-10: The house Mark Beaubien built at Lake and Wells in 1834, after he left the Sauganash. It is shown as it was in July 1835, with the people who ran it then. The building did not change. In August 1834 it was named the Exchange Coffee House. By 1836 Abram A. Markle's name was on it. Later the sign said Illinois Exchange. Those were changes of name and use.
11-13: The house Mark Beaubien built at Lake and Wells in 1834 after leaving the Sauganash, as it stood in July 1835 with the keepers it had then. The building did not change. It was named the Exchange Coffee House in August 1834. Abram A. Markle's name was on it by 1836, and later the sign said "Illinois Exchange." Those were changes of use and of sign.
14-15: The house Mark Beaubien built at Lake and Wells in 1834 after leaving the Sauganash, as it stood in July 1835 and with the keepers it had then. Nothing here changes the building itself. Its naming as the Exchange Coffee House in August 1834, Abram A. Markle's name on it by 1836, and the later sign "Illinois Exchange" are changes of use and of sign.

8-10: The house Alanson Sweet built in 1833. Ira Couch ran it in July 1835. No one wrote that the building changed. A history book tells only who ran it. First Sweet and a man from Canada named Darwin, then the Couch brothers, then James Couch from 1836. So it is shown in one look from 1833 to 1839. That is because we know so little. It does not mean nothing changed. Its three floors with shutters come from a picture by Gifford that the owner liked. The picture does not tell when each part was added. A smaller house of two floors is also possible. No dates are made up.
11-13: The house Alanson Sweet built in 1833, run by Ira Couch in July 1835. No change to the building is recorded. Andreas gives only who ran it: Sweet and a man from Canada named Darwin, then the Couch brothers, then James Couch from 1836. So the years 1833 to 1839 are shown as one look. That is a gap in what we know, not a claim that nothing changed. The three-story look with shutters comes from Gifford's picture, which the owner approved. The picture does not say when each part was added, and no date is made up. A smaller two-story reading of Gale's words is kept on its own.
14-15: The house Alanson Sweet built in 1833, kept by Ira Couch in July 1835. No change to the building is recorded. Andreas records only changes of who ran it: Sweet and a man from Canada named Darwin, then the Couch brothers, then James Couch from 1836. So 1833 to 1839 is modelled as one state. That is a limit of the evidence, not a claim that nothing changed. The three-story form comes from the Gifford picture the owner approved, read as looking back. The picture does not show when each part was added, and no date is invented. The three-story form with shutters is the main reading. A smaller two-story reading of Gale's words is kept on its own, and no order of growth is claimed.

8-10: The house as it stood from 1833. It was Dexter Graves's log inn of 1831. It stood back from Lake Street. That year he built a wood part across its front, out to the street. The old log inn is not shown on its own. We do not know how far back it stood. Showing it would mean making up a number. Some changes do not count either. Graves sold it to his son-in-law, Edward Haddock, around 1833. Haddock ran it until 1835. Then Abram A. Markle ran it for two years. Those were changes in who ran it, not in the house.
The house as the ad tells of it. It had four rooms, a kitchen, a barn and a garden. The ad says only that it was at Wabansia.
11-13: The house as the ad describes it: four rooms, a kitchen, a barn and a garden. The ad names the land only as Wabansia.
14-15: The house as the advertisement describes it: four rooms, a kitchen, a barn and a garden, on land the ad names only as Wabansia.

8-10: A house in the row on the west bank in the early 1830s. No one wrote that it changed. In fact, no one wrote how it looked at all. So it is shown in one look. That does not mean it stayed the same.
11-13: A house in the row on the west bank in the early 1830s. No change is recorded, because nothing about how it looked is recorded at all. It is one look because there is nothing to split it into, not because it is known to have stayed the same.

8-10: A house on Michigan Street between Cass and Rush. John Watkins used it for his second school in 1833. It is shown as a house, because that is what it was. Nothing in it was built for a school. No one wrote of a school room, a bench or a desk. We do not know if it was still there in July 1835, or if anyone still taught in it.
11-13: The house on the north side of Michigan Street between Cass and Rush that John Watkins used for his second school in 1833. It is shown as a house, because a house is what it was. Nothing in it was built for teaching, and no source tells of a school room, a bench or a desk. Whether it still stood in July 1835, and whether anyone taught in it then, is not known.

8-10: A house on North Water Street in 1835. John Davis ran it as the Steamboat Hotel. In November 1835 new men took it over. In 1836 it got a new name, the American Hotel. Those were changes in use, not in the house.
11-13: The house on North Water Street in 1835, run as the Steamboat Hotel by John Davis. New managers took over in November 1835, and in 1836 it was renamed the American Hotel under William McCorrister. Those were changes of use, not of the building.
14-15: The house on North Water Street in 1835, kept as the Steamboat Hotel by John Davis. The new managers of November 1835, J. Dorsey and J. Force, and the new name of American Hotel under William McCorrister in 1836 are changes of use. They do not start new stages.

8-10: A house for sale at the corner of LaSalle and Lake. The town paper had an ad for it. It was sixteen feet by thirty and cost $250. The buyer could move in on the first of the month. It stood on the one corner there that was still empty. The size comes from the paper. The corner, the floors and the look are guesses.
11-13: The house the Chicago Democrat offered for sale at the corner of LaSalle and Lake: sixteen by thirty feet, $250, ready on the first of the month. It stands on the one corner of that crossing that was still empty. The size is from the paper. The corner, the floors and the finish are not.
14-15: The house the Chicago Democrat offered for sale at LaSalle and Lake: sixteen by thirty feet, $250, move in on the first of the month. It stands on the one corner of that crossing the town had left empty. The size is the paper's. The corner, the stories and the finish are not.

8-10: The big stable behind W. H. Stow's Western Hotel, at Randolph and Canal. It stood across the wagon yard from the back of the hotel. No one wrote how it was built. We only know it was big, it was in back, and wagon trains pulled into the yard in front of it from two streets.
11-13: The large stable behind W. H. Stow's Western Hotel at Randolph and Canal, across the wagon yard from the back of the house. Nothing is recorded about how it was built. What is known is that it was large, that it was at the back, and that the yard in front of it took wagon trains in from two streets.

8-10: The log building that Father Walker put up at Wolf Point. It was used for church and for school. It was here by 1831. The Methodists who met here formed a group on 14 June 1831. No one wrote that it changed. In 1838 it was moved across the river, to Washington and Clark.
11-13: The log building Father Walker put up at Wolf Point for church and school. It stood by 1831, and the Methodist group formed on 14 June 1831 used it. No change to it is recorded. This stage ends with its move across the river to Washington and Clark in 1838.
14-15: The log building Father Walker put up at Wolf Point for worship and school. It stood by 1831 and was used by the Methodist group formed on 14 June 1831. No change to it is recorded in this stage. The stage ends with the 1838 move across the river to Washington and Clark. That is a change of place, which would start a new stage if the later site were ever built.

8-10: The log cabins in the row on the west bank at Wolf Point in 1831. They stood between Wentworth's inn and the log church to the north. This shows only the cabins. It does not say who lived in them in July 1835.

The log council house on the north bank, in the years around 1835. In 1834 the Methodists held church here while they built their own. On 18 August 1835 a big meeting gathered here. Those were uses of the house. This shows only the building.
11-13: The log council house on the north bank in the two years before and after July 1835. The Methodists held services here in 1834 while they built their own church. The meeting of 18 August 1835 gathered here. Those are its uses. This record shows only the building.
14-15: The log council house standing on the north bank in the two years either side of July 1835. The Methodists held services in it in 1834 while they built their own house, and the meeting of 18 August 1835 gathered here. Its uses do not start new stages, and this record shows only the building.

8-10: The log house where Eliza Chappel had her school for small children in 1833 and 1834. It had a school room and a place to live. It stood just west of the fort's land. In 1834 the school moved to the church at Lake and Clark. This shows the building. We think it still stood in July 1835. We do not know what it was used for then.
11-13: The log house where Eliza Chappel ran her school for young children in 1833 and 1834. It was split into a school room and living rooms. It stood just west of the fort's land. In 1834 the school moved to the First Presbyterian Church at Lake and Clark. This shows the building, which we think still stood in July 1835. What it was used for then is not known.
14-15: The log house Eliza Chappel's school for young children used in 1833 and 1834. It was split into a school room and living rooms, just west of the fort's land. The school left in 1834 for the First Presbyterian Church at Lake and Clark. This stage carries the building, which probably still stood on 1 July 1835. It makes no claim about what it was used for then.

8-10: The log house John Miller built in 1831, just north of his brother's inn. He used it to make leather. It was the first shop of its kind in the town. In 1832 Benjamin Hall became his partner. That was a change in the business, not in the house.
11-13: The log house John Miller built in 1831 just north of his brother's inn. He used it to tan leather, the town's first known workshop. Benjamin Hall became his partner in 1832. That was a change of business, not of the building.
14-15: The log house John Miller built in 1831 just north of his brother's tavern and used as a tannery, the town's first recorded workshop. Benjamin Hall's arrival as his partner in 1832 is a change of business. It does not start a new stage.

8-10: The log building where meat was cut, from 1827 to 1834. A history book says it was still used in 1833. Later, a wood one of Clybourne's stood here, by 1883. No one knows when that changed. So this shows the log building only. At first it made meat for the fort. Later it sold meat to others. That was a change in business, not in the building.
11-13: The log slaughterhouse as it stood from 1827 through 1834. Andreas says it was still the working plant in 1833. By 1883 a wood slaughterhouse of Clybourne's stood on the spot. Nothing dates the change, so this shows the log building and stops there. Its move from meat for the fort to meat for sale was a change of business, not of the building.

8-10: A log store at the west end of a block on Lake Street. On 31 March 1831 Chicago got a post office. For three years it was in this store. One side was the post office. The other side was a store. From 1833 John Bates Jr. sorted the mail. In July 1834 the post office moved to Franklin and South Water. So in July 1835 this is not the post office.
11-13: The log store at the west end of the Lake Street block. When Chicago got its post office on 31 March 1831, it was here, and it stayed for three years. The store was split, with the post office on one side and the store of Brewster, Hogan and Company on the other. John Bates Jr. sorted the mail from 1833. The post office moved to Franklin and South Water in about July 1834. That was a change of use, and it is why this is not the post office in July 1835.
14-15: The log store at the west end of the Lake Street block when the United States opened a post office at Chicago on 31 March 1831. For three years it held the post office, split in two: the post office on one side and the store of Brewster, Hogan and Company on the other. John Bates Jr. sorted the mail from 1833. The post office moved to Franklin and South Water about July 1834. That is a change of use, and it does not start a new stage. It is why this building is not the post office in July 1835.

8-10: The office of the Chicago American. T. O. Davis started the paper on 8 June 1835. On 1 July it is just over three weeks old. It came out once a week, on Saturday mornings. Each sheet was about 15 by 21 inches, with six rows of print. It was printed on South Water Street, near the bridge at Dearborn. That was three blocks east of the other paper, the Chicago Democrat.
11-13: The office of the Chicago American, started by T. O. Davis on 8 June 1835. In July 1835 it is twenty-three days old. It was a weekly paper on a sheet 15.5 by 21.5 inches, with six columns. It came out on Saturday mornings. It was printed on South Water Street near the Dearborn Street bridge, three blocks east of the Chicago Democrat's office at Clark.
14-15: The office of the Chicago American, started by T. O. Davis on 8 June 1835, twenty-three days before 1 July. It was a weekly on a sheet 15.5 by 21.5 inches, six columns, out on Saturday mornings. It was printed on South Water Street near the south end of the Dearborn Street drawbridge, three blocks east of the Chicago Democrat's twenty-month-old office at Clark.

8-10: The north pier as it was in the summer of 1835. It was a line of wood boxes filled with stone. It ran out into the lake from the north bank. It was about nine hundred feet long. It got longer every month. This shows just one moment.
11-13: The north pier in the summer of 1835. It was a line of timber cribs running out into the lake from the north bank, about nine hundred feet long. It grew longer every month, so this is one moment in time.

8-10: The south pier as it was in the summer of 1835. It was a line of wood boxes filled with stone. It ran out into the lake from the shore by the fort. It was about four hundred feet long. Before the fall, five hundred feet more would be added. It got longer every month. This shows just one moment.
11-13: The south pier in the summer of 1835. It was a line of timber cribs running out into the lake from the shore by the fort, about four hundred feet long. Before the season ended, five hundred feet more would be added. It grew longer every month, so this is one moment in time.
14-15: The one stage this record has: the south pier in the summer of 1835. It was a line of timber cribs running east-south-east from the shore on the south side of the cut, about four hundred feet long. It was about to grow by five hundred more before the season closed. It is a snapshot of something that got longer every month.

8-10: The plain wood church of the First Presbyterian people. It stood at Lake and Clark. It opened on 4 January 1834. It was 40 by 25 feet and cost $600. It had pine benches for about 200 people. The walls were plastered. The floors were rough logs split flat. It had no tower. People say almost everyone in town helped build it. No one wrote that it changed.
11-13: The plain wood church the First Presbyterian people built at Lake and Clark. It opened on 4 January 1834. It was 40 by 25 feet and cost $600. It had pine benches for about 200, plaster walls, rough split-log floors and no tower. Almost everyone in town is said to have helped build it. No change to it is recorded.

8-10: The meat plant as it was built in 1834 and used that year. No one wrote that it changed. In fact, after the line that says it was built, nothing tells of it at all.
11-13: The plant as it was built in 1834 and worked that season. No change to it is recorded, because nothing describes it at all after the line that records its building.

8-10: The shop Frederick Thomas had ads for in the summer of 1835. We know where it was in an odd way. Not by a corner, and not by a block. We count doors from the paper's office next door.
11-13: Frederick Thomas had ads for this shop in the summer of 1835. Its place is found in an odd way. It is not by a corner or by a block. It is by counting doors along the street from the paper's office.
14-15: The shop Frederick Thomas advertised from in the summer of 1835. It is placed in a way no other building here is: not by a corner, not by a block, but by counting doors from the newspaper office next along the street.

8-10: The shop as an ad in one paper tells of it in November 1833. Three ads in the other paper carry it on to July 1835. It is the same shop and the same trade. But now one man runs it, not two. Nothing about the building changes. Its place, size and look stay the same. What changes is how sure we are of the dates, and the name over the door.
11-13: The shop as the Democrat's ad opens it in November 1833 and as three ads in the American carry it to July 1835. It is the same shop and the same trade, with one owner instead of two. Nothing about the building changes. Its place, size and shape stay just as they were. What changes is how sure the dates are, and the name over the door.
14-15: The shop as the Democrat's ad opens it in November 1833 and as the American's three printings carry it to July 1835. It is the same shop and the same trade, with one owner instead of two. Nothing about the building changes here: its place, footprint and form stay as they were, and the American settles none of them. What changes is how sure the dates are, and the name over the door.

8-10: The shop at its bigger size, as it was in July 1835. A history book says the owner "was soon obliged to enlarge his shop." But it gives no date and no size. So it is shown in one look, not two. Two looks would mean making up a date and two sizes. That is three made-up things for one sentence. If a date turns up, we can split it then.
11-13: The shop at its bigger size, which is how it was in July 1835. Andreas says "he was soon obliged to enlarge his shop," but gives no date and no size before or after. So it is one stage, not two. A second stage would mean making up the date, the size before and the size after. That is three made-up things for one sentence. If a date turns up, it can be split then.
14-15: The shop at its enlarged size, the state July 1835 needs. Andreas records the enlargement, "he was soon obliged to enlarge his shop," with no date and no size at either stage. So it is kept as one stage, not two. A second stage would have to invent the date, the size before and the size after: three inventions for one sentence. If a date ever turns up, the stage can be split then.

8-10: This bridge has one look only. A history book says it was fixed in 1835 and again in 1837. In September 1834 the town paid $166.67 for repairs. That was just weeks after it was built. So in July 1835 the bridge was patched. Boats had hit it many times. No one wrote enough about the fixes to show a second look. So it is shown as one worn bridge.
11-13: The only stage this bridge has. Andreas says it was repaired in 1835 and again in 1837. A payment of $166.67 for repairs in September 1834 shows it needed work within weeks of being built. So the bridge in July 1835 was patched and had been hit many times by passing boats. No source describes the repairs well enough for a second stage. So this shows one look, and says here that it was a worn one.
14-15: The single stage this bridge has. Andreas records it as repaired in 1835 and again in 1837, and the September 1834 payment of $166.67 for repairs shows it needed work within weeks of being accepted. So the bridge standing on 1 July 1835 was patched and had been struck many times by passing boats. No source dates or describes those repairs well enough for a second stage. The record shows one state and says here that it was a worn one.

8-10: This bridge has one look only. It was a log bridge on log boxes at each end. It carried Kinzie Street over the North Branch of the river. In 1832 there was a walkway here. We do not know when it changed. So it is shown in one look, as it was in 1835.
11-13: The only stage this bridge has: a log bridge resting on log cribs at each end, carrying Kinzie Street across the North Branch. The 1832 walkway and what it had become by 1835 are shown as one stage, because no source dates the change. The bridge is shown as it was in 1835, and the record says so.
14-15: The single stage this structure has: a log beam bridge on cribbed ends, carrying the Kinzie Street line across the North Branch. The 1832 walkway and whatever it became by 1835 are shown as one stage, because no source dates the change. Its form takes the 1835 reading, and the record says so.

8-10: This bridge has one look only. It was a log bridge on log ends, with two log frames in the middle. It crossed the South Branch of the river, between Lake and Randolph. It has one look because no one wrote that it changed. Also, we only know of it for two and a half years.
11-13: The only stage this bridge has: a log bridge on log ends and two log frames, crossing the South Branch between Lake and Randolph. It is one stage because no source dates any change to it. And everything known about it covers only two and a half years.

8-10: The small store Philo Carpenter built in the summer of 1833. It was on South Water Street, between LaSalle and Wells. He was Chicago's first druggist, and this was his second shop. Because of it, his old log shop of 1832 on Lake Street may not have still stood. In July 1835 this store is two years old.
11-13: The small store Philo Carpenter built in the summer of 1833 on South Water Street, between LaSalle and Wells. It was the second shop of Chicago's first druggist. It makes it unlikely that his 1832 log shop on Lake Street still stood. In July 1835 it is two years old.
14-15: The small store Philo Carpenter built in the summer of 1833 on a lot he had bought on South Water Street between LaSalle and Wells. It was the second shop of Chicago's first druggist, and it makes it doubtful that his 1832 log shop on Lake Street survived. In July 1835 it is two years old.

8-10: The wall of the second Fort Dearborn. It was made of tall, sharp logs in a square. There were lookout corners at two sides, and a block house at one corner. Big gates opened to the north and the south. In July 1835 soldiers were still here. Major John Greene was in charge.

The store of Harmon and Loomis at the corner of Clark and South Water. It was open in the middle 1830s. It sold cloth, dishes, tools, food and drink. It also sold leather and saddles for other people. In 1839 a building of three floors stood on this corner. A paper was printed on its top floor. We do not know if this store had grown, or if it was a new building. So the 1835 store is not made that tall.
11-13: The store of Harmon and Loomis at Clark and South Water, open through the middle 1830s. It sold dry goods, dishes, hardware, food and drink, and leather and saddles for others. In 1839 a three-story building on this corner had the Daily Chicago American on its top floor. Whether that was this store grown taller or a new building is not known. So the 1835 store takes none of its height.
14-15: The store of Harmon and Loomis at the corner of Clark and South Water, trading through the mid-1830s. It sold dry goods, dishes, hardware, wet and dry groceries, and leather and saddles on commission. In 1839 a three-story building on this corner had the Daily Chicago American on its top floor. Whether that was this building grown or a new one is not recorded, and the 1835 store takes none of its height on purpose.

8-10: A store house in the row on the west bank in the early 1830s. No one wrote that it changed. No one wrote how it looked at all. After the treaty of 1833, trade with the Native people fell away. That was a change in business, not in the building.

The inn as it stood in the 1830s. It was a log building. By the early 1830s a wood part was added. By about 1833 a painted wolf sign hung outside. No one wrote that it changed after that. So it is shown in one look from 1828 to 1836. That is because we know so little. It does not mean nothing changed.
11-13: The tavern as it stood through the 1830s: a log building that had gained a wood part by the early 1830s, with a painted wolf sign hung outside by about 1833. No change is recorded, so all of 1828 to 1836 is shown as one look. That is a gap in what we know, not a claim that nothing changed.
14-15: The tavern as it stood through the 1830s: a log building that had gained a frame part by the early 1830s, with the painted wolf sign hung outside by about 1833. No change to it is recorded in this stage, so all of 1828 to 1836 is one state. That is a limit of the evidence, not a claim that nothing changed.

8-10: A wood building two floors high, near Franklin and South Water. Dr. John T. Temple asked people to give money for it. It went up in the summer of 1833 and cost about $900. Church was held downstairs, and school upstairs. It was ready by 16 August 1833. Three churches took turns using it until January 1834. From December 1833 a school for boys used the upper floor. No one wrote that it changed.
11-13: The two-story wood building that Dr. John T. Temple's fund put up near Franklin and South Water in the summer of 1833. Church was held below and school above, and it cost about $900. It was ready by 16 August 1833. Methodists, Presbyterians and Baptists took turns in it until the Presbyterian church opened in January 1834. From December 1833 Grenville T. Sproat's school for boys used the upper floor. No change to it is recorded.
14-15: The two-story wood building Dr. John T. Temple's fund put up near Franklin and South Water in the summer of 1833: church below, school above, about $900. It was ready for use by 16 August 1833. Methodists, Presbyterians and Baptists used it in turn until the Presbyterian church opened in January 1834. Grenville T. Sproat's English and Classical School for Boys used the upper floor from December 1833. No change to it is recorded in this stage.

8-10: A wood hotel, two floors high, on Lake Street near Wells. Lathrop Johnson and George Stevens ran it. Its roof edge faced the street. It was built in 1834. By June 1835 it was open, and it rented rooms for offices. Two shops that put ads in the paper gave it as their address.
11-13: The two-story wood hotel Lathrop Johnson and George Stevens ran on the north side of Lake Street near Wells, with its long side to the street. It went up in 1834, and by June 1835 it was open and renting office rooms. Two of the American's advertisers gave it as their address.

8-10: P. F. W. Peck's store at the corner of South Water and LaSalle. It was made of wood and was two floors high. He lived here too. Downstairs he sold cloth, tools and food. Upstairs was a loft that was not finished, where people slept. This is where Peck is in July 1835. His other house and his brick house both came later, in 1837.
11-13: The two-story wood store P. F. W. Peck ran at the corner of South Water and LaSalle, and lived in. Downstairs he sold dry goods, hardware and food. Upstairs, an unfinished loft served as a place to sleep. This is where Peck is shown in July 1835. His two-story house at LaSalle and Washington and his brick house both date from 1837.
14-15: The two-story wood store P. F. W. Peck kept at the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle, and lived in. Dry goods, hardware and groceries were sold below, and an unfinished loft above served for sleeping. This is where Peck is shown on 1 July 1835, because his house at LaSalle and Washington comes from an 1837 account and his brick house is from 1837. Both are already left out on purpose.

8-10: A two-floor house facing the river, with a lower log cabin next to it. Together they make one home. An old drawing shows them side by side, so that is how they stand now. The drawing does not tell when it got bigger. In 1830 it became an inn. After 1832 it was a store again. In 1834 Miller left. Those were changes in use, not in the house.
11-13: The two-story house facing the river and the lower log cabin next to it make up one home. The old drawing shows them side by side, so that replaces the old idea of one in front of the other. A drawing made later does not date when it grew. It became an inn in 1830, went back to a store after 1832, and Miller left in 1834. Those were changes of use.
14-15: The two-story river-facing house and the lower log cabin beside it make up one house. The side-by-side drawing replaces the earlier idea of one behind the other. A drawing made years later does not date an enlargement. Its change to a tavern in 1830, its return to a store after 1832 and the end of Miller's part in 1834 are changes of use. They do not start new stages.

8-10: The warehouse in the river trade of 1834 and 1835. No one wrote when it was built, or how it changed. So it is shown in one look. That is because we know so little. In August 1835 one man put it on the north bank. The owner later moved it out of the road to the corner of Franklin and South Water. It still faces the river.

The wood sale room John Bates Jr. built on Dearborn Street in 1833 or 1834. It was between Lake and South Water. It was where the town sold things, back when the town was selling its own land. In October 1833 Bates ran a big land sale. It turned the land south of Madison into lots. He also helped run the post office from that year.
11-13: The wood auction room John Bates Jr. put up on the west side of Dearborn, between Lake and South Water, in 1833 or 1834. It was the town's sale room, in the years when the town was selling itself. Bates called the school land sale of October 1833 that turned the land south of Madison into lots. He was also the deputy postmaster from that year.
14-15: The wooden auction room John Bates Jr. put up on the west side of Dearborn between Lake and South Water in 1833 or 1834. It was the town's sale room, in the years when the town was selling itself. Bates called the school-section sale of October 1833, which turned the section south of Madison into lots. He was deputy postmaster from the same year.

8-10: The yard as it was set up in the spring of 1833 and used through 1835. No one wrote that it changed. After the line that says it was set up, nothing tells of it at all.
11-13: The yard as it was set up in the spring of 1833 and worked through 1833, 1834 and 1835. Nothing describes any change to it. In fact, nothing describes it at all after the line that records its start.

8-10: A wood part, two floors high. It was built onto the log cabin at Lake and Market in 1831. Then the whole place was called the Sauganash Hotel. It was the first hotel in Chicago.
11-13: A two-story wood building built onto the log cabin at the Lake and Market corner in 1831. The whole was then called the Sauganash Hotel, Chicago's first hotel.
14-15: A two-story frame building added onto the log cabin at the Lake and Market corner in 1831. The whole was then known as the Sauganash Hotel, Chicago's first hotel.
